## 1. Lorentz Force Law (Classical Electrodynamics)

The fundamental equation underlying all magnetic force claims in this dataset:

F = q(E + v × B)

Components:
* F: electromagnetic force on charge carrier [N]
* q: electric charge [C] (q = −e for electron, q = +Ze for ion of atomic number Z)
* E: electric field vector [V/m]
* v: velocity vector of charge carrier [m/s]
* B: magnetic flux density vector [T]
* ×: cross product (produces force perpendicular to both v and B)

Magnetic-only Lorentz force (E = 0 case):
F_mag = q(v × B)

This is the basis for:
* Circular/helical trajectories of charged particles in magnetic fields.
* Motor torque on current-carrying conductors.
* The claimed upward reaction force on the spinning magnet from deflected ionized air.

---

## 2. Rotating Magnetic Field — Three-Phase Stator

For a 3-phase, p-pole-pair stator with coils at angular positions θ_k = 2π(k-1)/n_coils, k = 1,...,n_coils, carrying currents:

I_k(t) = I_0 cos(ωt − 2π(k-1)/3) [for n_coils = 6, UVW-UVW pattern, alternating phases]

The resultant magnetic flux density at azimuthal angle θ in the air gap:

B(θ, t) = (3/2) B_0 cos(ωt − pθ) [forward-traveling wave, fundamental]

plus harmonic terms:
B_harmonic(θ, t) = Σ_n B_n cos(ωt ± npθ) [backward and forward harmonics]

where:
* ω = 2πf [rad/s], f = supply frequency [Hz]
* p = pole pair number (= 3 for 6-coil UVW-UVW winding)
* B_0 = peak flux density per phase [T]

For the observed UVW-UVW, 6-coil geometry: p = 3 → three full flux cycles around the stator circumference.

---

## 3. Rotor Synchronous Speed

For synchronous operation (rotor locking to stator rotating field):

n_s = f / p [rev/s]   or   ω_s = ω / p [rad/s]

For contra-rotation to the fundamental (backward wave locking):

n_contra = −f / p = −n_s [rev/s] (opposite sign convention)

Drew's 8-magnet N-S-N-S rotor has p_rotor = 4 pole pairs. The mismatch:
Δp = p_rotor − p_stator = 4 − 3 = 1

The rotor may interact with the (p_stator ± p_rotor) = (3 ± 4) spatial harmonics of the stator field:
* p = 7 harmonic: forward-traveling, slow.
* p = −1 harmonic (i.e., p = 1 backward): backward-traveling component.

If the backward p = 1 component is significant, the rotor could lock to it and contra-rotate at:
n_contra = −f/1 = −f [rev/s]

This is a much higher speed than the fundamental synchronous speed n_s = f/3, which may explain the energetic nature of the observed contra-rotation.

---

## 4. Torque in a Magnetic Motor

General expression for electromagnetic torque on a rotor:

τ = (p/2) × (3/2) × (L_d − L_q) I_d I_q + (p/2) × (3/2) × λ_f I_q

For a surface permanent magnet motor (SPMSM, where L_d ≈ L_q):
τ ≈ (3p/4) λ_f I_q

where:
* p = pole pair count
* L_d, L_q = d-axis and q-axis inductances [H]
* I_d, I_q = d-axis and q-axis current components [A]
* λ_f = flux linkage from permanent magnets [Wb]

For the contra-rotating configuration, this formula applies with a negative effective Ω_r (rotor angular velocity), meaning the torque direction is reversed relative to standard operation.

---

## 5. Homopolar Motor / Faraday Disk EMF

For a conducting disk of radius R rotating at angular velocity ω_disk in uniform axial magnetic field B_axial:

EMF = (1/2) ω_disk B_axial R²

Torque for drive current I through the disk:
τ_homo = (1/2) I B_axial R²

Power:
P = τ_homo × ω_disk = (1/2) I B_axial R² ω_disk = EMF × I

For the liquid metal variant (replacing solid disk with conducting liquid of conductivity σ_liquid):
* Current density: J = σ_liquid (E + v × B) [A/m²]
* Body force density: f = J × B [N/m³]
* Net torque from integration over liquid volume V:
τ_MHD = ∫_V (r × (J × B)) dV

where r is the position vector from the rotation axis.

---

## 6. Gyroscope Precession Rate

For a gyroscope of:
* Mass M
* Spin angular velocity ω (about spin axis, aligned with symmetry axis)
* Moment of inertia about spin axis: I_spin
* Center of mass offset from pivot: r [m]

Precession angular velocity:
Ω_p = Mgr / (I_spin ω) = τ_gravity / L

where L = I_spin ω = angular momentum magnitude, τ_gravity = Mgr = gravitational torque magnitude.

As ω → ∞: Ω_p → 0 (gyroscope stabilizes vertically).
As ω → 0: Ω_p → ∞ (gyroscope falls chaotically).

Drew's anti-gravity hypothesis requires identifying a term F_z(ω) such that:
F_z = dL_z/dt > 0 for increasing ω

In standard mechanics, for a gyroscope precessing about a vertical axis:
L_z = I_spin ω cos(θ) + I_transverse Ω_p sin(θ) cos(θ)

where θ = nutation angle. For constant θ and ω increasing, L_z increases, but the required torque τ_z = dL_z/dt must come from somewhere — the pivot reaction force. If the pivot is replaced by the ground reaction on a craft, an increasing L_z would manifest as an increasing reaction force at the ground contact — consistent with apparent weight reduction (anti-gravity).

---

## 7. Periodic Lift Force from Oscillating Coupled Flywheels

For two magnetically coupled counter-spinning flywheels, each of moment of inertia I and magnetic moment m, spinning at ±ω:

Magnetic interaction energy between two aligned dipoles at separation d:
U(d, φ) = (μ₀/4π) [m₁·m₂/d³ − 3(m₁·r̂)(m₂·r̂)/d³]

where φ = relative azimuthal angle between the dipoles.

For counter-spinning flywheels, φ(t) = 2ωt (relative angle advances at twice the spin rate). The interaction energy oscillates at 2ω:
U(t) = U_0 cos(2ωt + φ_0)

The vertical force between the two flywheels:
F_z = −∂U/∂d = F_0(d) cos(2ωt + φ_0)

The time-averaged vertical force is zero for symmetric counter-spinning. However, if the oscillation is asymmetric (different pole strengths above vs. below, or offset geometry), a net bias emerges:

<F_z> = (1/T) ∫₀ᵀ F_z(t) dt ≠ 0

This net time-averaged vertical force is the proposed lift mechanism. The "periodic upward motion" described by Drew corresponds to the positive half-cycles of this oscillating F_z.

---

## 8. Comet Nucleus Rotation — Angular Momentum Constraints

Source: claimed rotation period of 3I/ATLAS core = minutes.

For a spherical comet nucleus of radius R and density ρ rotating at angular velocity ω_comet:
* Moment of inertia: I = (2/5) M R² = (2/5)(4πρR³/3)R² = (8π/15)ρR⁵
* Angular momentum: L = Iω_comet = (8π/15)ρR⁵ω_comet
* Centrifugal surface acceleration: a_c = ω_comet² R
* Gravitational surface acceleration: g_s = GM/R² = G(4πρR³/3)/R² = (4π/3)GρR

For structural integrity (centrifugal breakup limit):
a_c < g_s → ω_comet² R < (4π/3)GρR → ω_comet < √[(4π/3)Gρ]

For ρ = 500 kg/m³ (typical comet density):
ω_max = √[(4π/3)(6.674×10⁻¹¹)(500)] ≈ √(1.4×10⁻⁷) ≈ 3.75×10⁻⁴ rad/s
T_min = 2π/ω_max ≈ 16,750 s ≈ 4.6 hours

For a rotation period of minutes (say T = 5 min = 300 s):
ω_required = 2π/300 ≈ 0.021 rad/s

Ratio: ω_required/ω_max ≈ 56 — requiring centrifugal acceleration 56² ≈ 3,136 times stronger than gravitational cohesion.

This means: a natural cometary body CANNOT rotate with a period of minutes without flying apart, unless it is either:
1. Made of anomalously high-density, high-tensile material (non-ice composition), or
2. An artificial rigid structure with sufficient internal binding strength.

This is the mathematical basis for Drew's claim that 3I/ATLAS's fast-spinning core implies artificiality.

---

## 9. Ionization Voltage and Plasma Formation

Applied voltage for ionization: 6.6 kV (stated in referenced tweet).

Paschen's Law for air breakdown:
V_breakdown = B(pd) / [ln(pd) + ln(A) − ln(ln(1 + 1/γ_se))]

where:
* p = gas pressure [Pa]
* d = electrode gap [m]
* A ≈ 12 (cm·Pa)⁻¹, B ≈ 365 V/(cm·Pa) for air
* γ_se = secondary electron emission coefficient

At atmospheric pressure (p = 101,325 Pa = 760 Torr), the Paschen minimum for air:
V_min ≈ 330 V at pd ≈ 0.75 Torr·cm

For V = 6,600 V at atmospheric pressure:
pd = V/B × f(pd) → gap d ≈ several mm to cm (depending on electrode geometry)

The 6.6 kV excitation produces glow discharge or streamer discharge in air, creating a weakly ionized plasma suitable for MHD interaction with the magnet's rotating field.

---

## 10. Motional EMF for Rotating Conducting Sphere

For a conducting sphere of radius a rotating at angular velocity ω about its symmetry axis (z-axis) in an external magnetic field B = B_0 ẑ:

The motional EMF induced along any radius from center to surface:
ε = ∫₀ᵃ (v × B) · dr = ∫₀ᵃ (ωr × B_0 ẑ) · r̂ dr

For v = ωr sin(θ) φ̂ (azimuthal velocity at polar angle θ) and B = B_0 ẑ:
(v × B) = ωr sin(θ) B_0 (φ̂ × ẑ) = ωr sin(θ) B_0 (−r̂ sin(θ) + θ̂ cos(θ)) ... [spherical geometry]

Integrating along the equatorial radius (θ = π/2):
ε = ∫₀ᵃ ωr B_0 dr = (1/2) ω B_0 a²

This is the same result as the Faraday disk (homopolar generator), confirming the spherical conducting ball in the LED demonstration is operating on homopolar generator principles.

For a = 0.025 m (2.5 cm radius), B_0 = 0.1 T, ω = 100 rad/s:
ε = (1/2)(100)(0.1)(0.025²) = 3.125 × 10⁻³ V = 3.1 mV

To light an LED requires V_LED ≈ 1.8−3.5 V, so either:
* ω must be much higher (ω ≈ 57,600 rad/s for a 1.8 V LED), or
* Multiple turns / amplification stage used, or
* The demonstration uses a different source geometry with stronger B or more favorable geometry.

## 1. 3-Phase Rotating Magnetic Field — Mathematical Derivation

Source: YAML 2017877032907247916, YAML 2021005921309385050, MDX 13_2017872609355116544_video.mdx

### Phase Currents

Three coils displaced 120° apart in physical space carry currents:

    I_A(t) = I₀ sin(ωt)
    I_B(t) = I₀ sin(ωt + 2π/3)
    I_C(t) = I₀ sin(ωt + 4π/3)

Each coil i produces a magnetic field B_i(t) = B₀ sin(ωt + φᵢ) along its own axis n̂ᵢ,
where φ_A = 0, φ_B = 2π/3, φ_C = 4π/3.

Defining coil axes in the XY-plane:
    n̂_A = x̂,  n̂_B = -x̂/2 + √3ŷ/2,  n̂_C = -x̂/2 - √3ŷ/2

Total field (superposition):
    B(t) = B₀ [ sin(ωt) x̂
              + sin(ωt + 2π/3)(-x̂/2 + √3ŷ/2)
              + sin(ωt + 4π/3)(-x̂/2 - √3ŷ/2) ]

Expanding with trigonometric identities sin(A+B) = sinA cosB + cosA sinB:

    B_x(t) = B₀ [sin(ωt) - (1/2)sin(ωt + 2π/3) - (1/2)sin(ωt + 4π/3)]
            = B₀ sin(ωt) [1 - (1/2)cos(2π/3) - (1/2)cos(4π/3)]
            - B₀ cos(ωt) [(1/2)sin(2π/3) + (1/2)sin(4π/3)]
            = B₀ sin(ωt) [1 + 1/4 + 1/4] - B₀ cos(ωt) [√3/4 - √3/4]
            = (3/2) B₀ sin(ωt)

    B_y(t) = B₀ [(√3/2)sin(ωt + 2π/3) - (√3/2)sin(ωt + 4π/3)]
            = (√3 B₀/2) [sin(ωt + 2π/3) - sin(ωt + 4π/3)]
            Using sum-to-product: sin(A) - sin(B) = 2cos((A+B)/2)sin((A-B)/2)
            A+B = 2ωt + 2π, A-B = 2π/3... etc.
            Result: B_y(t) = -(3/2) B₀ cos(ωt)

    Therefore:
    B(t) = (3/2) B₀ [sin(ωt) x̂ - cos(ωt) ŷ]
          = (3/2) B₀ [cos(ωt - π/2) x̂ + cos(ωt + π) ŷ] ... (rotates clockwise)
    or equivalently (choosing phase convention):
    B(t) = (3/2) B₀ [cos(ωt) x̂ + sin(ωt) ŷ]  (counter-clockwise)

Magnitude: |B| = (3/2) B₀ = constant.

Conclusion: The 3-phase coil arrangement produces a rotating field of CONSTANT magnitude
(3/2)B₀ rotating at angular frequency ω in the XY-plane. This is the key mathematical
property distinguishing 3-phase from single-phase (which produces oscillating, not rotating,
field of varying magnitude).

## 2. Torque on Magnetic Dipole in Rotating Field

Source: YAML 2017877032907247916, YAML 1978591957686661487

### Synchronous Torque

A magnetic dipole moment m in field B experiences:
    τ = m × B

For a ring magnet spinning at angular velocity ω_m about Z-axis (synchronized to field):
    m = m (sin θ cos(ω_m t) x̂ + sin θ sin(ω_m t) ŷ + cos θ ẑ)

where θ is the angle between m and the Z-axis.

If ω_m = ω (synchronous): the torque τ = m × B(t) has a constant component in the ẑ direction
driving continuous rotation. The synchronous torque (pull-out torque) is:
    τ_max = m × (3/2) B₀

For the magnet to spin at ω, the applied field must supply enough torque to overcome friction
and any magnetic braking (homopolar effect).

## 3. Gyroscopic Precession — Force Redirection

Source: YAML 2017877032907247916 (note_tweet)

### Angular Momentum of Spinning Flywheel

    L = I Ω ẑ   (spinning flywheel, moment of inertia I, spin rate Ω)

where ẑ is the flywheel spin axis (vertical, for a horizontal flywheel).

### Applied Torque from Newton 3rd Law Reaction

If a downward force F_down = -F ẑ is applied at radius r from the flywheel center:
    τ_applied = r × F_down = r x̂ × (-F ẑ) = rF ŷ   (or similar, depending on direction)

### Resulting Precession

    dL/dt = τ_applied
    dΩ_precession / dt = τ_applied / |L| = rF / (I Ω)

Precession occurs in the horizontal (XY) plane, at angular velocity:
    Ω_p = τ_applied / |L| = rF / (I Ω)

Physical consequence: the downward force F_down causes the flywheel to precess horizontally,
NOT to move downward. The Z-component of motion is eliminated; the force is "redirected" into
the XY-plane as precession. This is the mechanism Drew proposes for cancelling the Newton
reaction force.

### Quantitative Condition for Full Redirection

For the precession to fully absorb the reaction without significant Z-axis displacement:
    Ω_p << Ω   (gyroscopic approximation valid)
    i.e., rF << I Ω²

This requires fast spin (large Ω) and/or large moment of inertia (large I) of the counter-
spinning flywheel. Drew states the flywheel must be "fast-spinning" for this to work.

If the circuit resistance is R_c:

The axial Lorentz force on the radial current in the field B_z:
    F_z = ∫ I_rad × B_z × 2πr dr / R  (integrated over disk)

Simplified: the electromagnetic braking torque on the disk is:

This opposes rotation (Lenz's law). The corresponding axial force component (the "Lorentz

## 2. 3-Phase Rotating Magnetic Field — Superposition

Standard electromagnetic result (not explicitly derived in sources but is the physical basis):

                m_k = -m_0 * z_hat for k = 2, 4, 6 (south-up, interleaved)

External field at large distances r >> R (ring radius):

  Leading term: quadrupole, decays as r^-5

inert to external ferromagnetic objects. The net magnetic moment is zero.

## 4. Critical Height for Levitation Equilibrium

Let F_z(h) = net upward electromagnetic force on rotor at height h above coil plane.

Equilibrium condition:
  F_z(h_c) = m_rotor * g

where h_c is the critical height.

For small perturbations about h_c:
  If dF_z/dh < 0 (force decreases with height, as expected for decaying coil field):
    The equilibrium is UNSTABLE: displacement upward gives F_z < m*g, rotor falls;
    displacement downward gives F_z > m*g, rotor rises back.
    This produces oscillation through h_c rather than stable hover.

Force-height dependence approximation (on-axis field of a coil ring of radius R at height h):
  B_z(h) = (mu_0 * n * I * R^2) / (2 * (R^2 + h^2)^(3/2))

  dB_z/dh = -3 * mu_0 * n * I * R^2 * h / (2 * (R^2 + h^2)^(5/2))  [negative for h > 0]

  The field gradient dB_z/dh is negative and its magnitude increases from h=0, peaks at h = R/2,
  then decreases. The lift force on a magnetic dipole m_z in a gradient field:
  F_z = m_z * dB_z/dh

  This reaches maximum near h ~ R/sqrt(2) and falls off for h >> R. So h_c satisfies:
    m_z * dB_z/dh |_{h=h_c} = m_rotor * g

  For standard parameters (R ~ 30-40 mm coil radius, m_z ~ few mJ/T for a 70mm disc magnet),
  h_c would be on the order of a few mm to ~2 cm above the coil plane.

## II. Magnetic Dipole Force Equations

### Static Dipole-Dipole Force (Axial Configuration)

The force on a magnetic dipole m_2 in the field of a dipole m_1 at axial separation r:

F_axial = (μ_0 / 4π) × (6 m_1 m_2) / r^4

Components:
* μ_0 = 4π × 10^−7 T·m/A (magnetic permeability of free space)
* m_1, m_2 = magnetic dipole moments (A·m²)
* r = center-to-center separation (m)
* F_axial = force along the axis connecting the dipoles (N); positive = repulsive, negative = attractive

The factor r^−4 (vs. r^−2 for monopoles) means dipole forces fall off rapidly with distance.

For antiparallel moments (attractive alignment, as in the static iron ball + magnet case):
F_axial = −(μ_0 / 4π) × (6 m_1 m_2) / r^4 (attractive)

The energy:
U_dipole = −(μ_0 / 4π) × (2 m_1 · m_2) / r^3

### Dynamic (Counter-Rotating) Interaction: "Delta" Effect

No explicit equation provided by Drew. The transition from attraction to repulsion under counter-rotation implies:

F_total = F_dipole + F_delta(ω_rel)

Where F_delta is the spin-dependent correction term:
* F_delta = 0 when ω_rel = 0 (static case → standard dipole attraction dominates)
* F_delta > |F_dipole| when ω_rel > ω_c (critical relative angular velocity → repulsion dominates)

The magnitude and functional form of F_delta are not specified in the source material. Drew describes it as experimental ("new to physics on Earth") without providing a governing equation. The critical angular velocity ω_c is also not specified quantitatively.

## III. Rotating Magnetic Field (n-Phase AC)

### General Formula

For n-phase AC coils at angular positions φ_k = 2π k/n, k = 0, 1, ..., n−1, each carrying current I_k = I_0 cos(ωt − 2πk/n), the combined magnetic field at the center is:

B(t) = B_0 × Σ_k [cos(ωt − 2πk/n)] × [cos(2πk/n) x̂ + sin(2πk/n) ŷ]

For n ≥ 3, the sum simplifies (using trigonometric identities):
B(t) = (n/2) × B_0 × [cos(ωt) x̂ + sin(ωt) ŷ]

Components:
* B_0 = peak field per phase (T)
* n/2 = amplitude factor (increases with n)
* ω = 2πf = angular frequency of AC supply (rad/s)
* The field magnitude |B| = (n/2) B_0 = constant, rotating at ω

### 3-Phase vs. 5-Phase Comparison (from tweet 1969904219017900157)

Claim: "5-phase is more powerful than 3-phase"

Mathematically:
* n=3: |B| = (3/2) B_0 = 1.5 B_0
* n=5: |B| = (5/2) B_0 = 2.5 B_0

The 5-phase system produces 2.5/1.5 = 1.667× larger field amplitude for the same peak current per phase. Additionally, the harmonic content differs:

For n=3: the field contains 5th and 7th harmonic components (from winding imperfections).
For n=5: the field contains 9th and 11th harmonic components — smaller in magnitude and higher in frequency — resulting in a more nearly perfect circular rotating field.

The motor torque from a rotating field of amplitude B on a rotor with moment m:
τ = m × B × sin(δ)

where δ is the torque angle (load angle). For a given δ, τ ∝ B, so the 5-phase system produces 1.667× more torque at the same rotor moment.

## 3. Barnett Effect Quantification

### Classical Barnett Magnetization
    M_z = chi_m * omega_z / gamma_e

where:
    chi_m = magnetic susceptibility (dimensionless, ~10^3 - 10^5 for ferromagnets, relative to mu_0)
    omega_z = angular velocity about Z-axis [rad/s]
    gamma_e = gyromagnetic ratio = e / (2 m_e) = 8.794 x 10^10 rad/(s*T)

For a ferromagnetic disc (e.g., NdFeB permanent magnet) spinning at omega_z = 10^4 rad/s (approximately 95,000 RPM):
    M_z ~ chi_m * 10^4 / (8.794 x 10^10)

The contribution is very small unless chi_m is enormous (not the case for a hard permanent magnet, which has small susceptibility tensor). The Barnett effect in hard magnets is therefore negligible compared to the intrinsic remanent magnetization.

### Spin-Angular Momentum Coupling
For a single electron: mu_s = -g_s * mu_B * S / hbar, where g_s ~ 2, mu_B = 9.274 x 10^-24 J/T.

For a macroscopic ferromagnet with net spin angular momentum L_s:
    M = gamma_e * L_s

Conservation of total angular momentum (mechanical + spin):
    d/dt (L_mech + L_spin) = tau_external

When L_spin changes due to demagnetization or re-orientation, L_mech changes to compensate.

## 4. Magnetic Dipole Force and Gradient

The Kelvin force on a magnetic dipole m in an inhomogeneous field:
    F = nabla(m . B)

For a fixed dipole m_z in a field with axial gradient dB_z/dz:
    F_z = m_z * (dB_z/dz)

This is the mechanism of magnetic levitation in standard magnetostatics (e.g., Earnshaw's theorem applies: stable levitation of a purely diamagnetic or paramagnetic object requires active feedback or time-varying fields).

Earnshaw's theorem: no configuration of static magnetic fields can stably levitate a static magnetic dipole. Therefore:
- Passive levitation of a permanent magnet above another permanent magnet is impossible in static configuration (unstable in at least one DOF).
- Time-varying fields (rotating fields, AC fields) can circumvent Earnshaw's theorem and produce stable levitation (e.g., as in the Levitron, or rotating field levitators).

The author's counter-rotating field device is a time-varying field system and therefore is not a priori ruled out by Earnshaw's theorem from producing a net levitation effect.

Let:
    theta_inner(t) = -omega_inner * t  (anti-clockwise, negative sign convention)
    theta_outer(t) = +omega_outer * t  (clockwise, positive sign convention)

The relative angle between inner and outer elements:
    Delta_theta(t) = theta_inner - theta_outer = -(omega_inner + omega_outer) * t

This relative angle increases linearly in time — the inner and outer elements are never phase-locked unless omega_inner = omega_outer = 0. The composite magnetic field seen at an intermediate radius r (R1 < r < R2) samples both contributions with different phase relationships at each instant.

The composite B_phi at radius r:

This superposition is in general a quasi-periodic or beat-frequency field if omega_inner ≠ omega_outer, producing time-varying Lorentz forces on any conducting material at radius r.

From tweet 2027427280973402279 (note_tweet), the torque cancellation at the axis for N outer coils wired as k repetitions of U-V-W (where N = 3k) can be characterized as follows.

## 4. Angular Momentum Conservation

Total angular momentum of closed system (no external torque, tau_ext = 0):
  L_total = L_outer + L_inner = I_outer * omega_outer + I_inner * omega_inner = constant

For the inner-magnet spin flip (anti-clockwise -> clockwise):
  delta_omega_inner = -2 * omega_inner  (sign reversal)
  delta_L_inner = I_inner * (-2 * omega_inner)
  delta_L_outer = -delta_L_inner = I_inner * 2 * omega_inner
  omega_outer_new = omega_outer_old + (2 * I_inner * omega_inner) / I_outer

Numerical example (outer flywheel, 16 magnets):
  Let I_outer = (M_outer * R_outer^2) / 2  (thin ring approximation for flywheel)
  Let I_inner = (m_inner * r_inner^2) / 2  (disc)
  When omega_inner reverses: omega_outer increases by 2 * I_inner * omega_inner / I_outer

If I_outer >> I_inner: small change in omega_outer
If I_outer ~ I_inner: large coupled response (strong counter-spin)

Drew's device design intent: balance I_outer and I_inner to maximize angular momentum
exchange and (hoped) axial force coupling.

---

## 5. Three-Phase Rotating Field Mathematics

Three-phase currents:
  i_U(t) = I_m * cos(omega_e * t)
  i_V(t) = I_m * cos(omega_e * t - 2*pi/3)
  i_W(t) = I_m * cos(omega_e * t - 4*pi/3)

Magnetic flux from spatially distributed coils (U at phi=0, V at phi=2*pi/3, W at phi=4*pi/3):
  B(phi, t) = (3/2) * B_m * cos(omega_e * t - phi)

This is a traveling wave in the azimuthal (phi) direction, rotating at omega_e. For
a p-pole machine (p poles), synchronous mechanical speed:
  omega_s_mech = (2 / p) * omega_e

For Drew's four-set (four-pole, p=4) configuration:
  omega_s_mech = omega_e / 2

The phase sequence U-V-W-U-V-W determines the rotation direction. Counter-phase (U-W-V)
reverses rotation direction. Drew identifies this as "3-phase counter-spin" when the
outer rotating field drives the inner disc in the opposite direction at high frequencies.

Induced voltage in inner disc from rotating field:
  V_induced = -d/dt (integral B . dA) = omega_s * Phi_max * sin(omega_s * t - delta)

where delta is a phase angle determined by disc impedance.

---

## 6. Probability Calculation — 3I/ATLAS Orbital Statistics

Given three independent events (Avi Loeb framework):
  P_1 = 1/200   (planetary ecliptic proximity)
  P_2 = 1/20,000  (bypassing Mars, Venus, Jupiter closely)
  P_3 = 1/14   (perihelion behind Sun from Earth)

Joint probability (independence assumed):
  P = P_1 * P_2 * P_3 = (1/200) * (1/20,000) * (1/14)
  P = 1 / (200 * 20,000 * 14)
  P = 1 / 56,000,000
  P ~ 1.79 x 10^-8

Drew's interpretation: P < 2 x 10^-8 makes the null hypothesis (natural interloper) untenable.
No correction for multiple comparisons or a posteriori selection effects is applied.

---

## 7. Homopolar Generator EMF

For a disc of radius R rotating at angular velocity omega in axial field B_z:
  EMF = (1/2) * B_z * omega * R^2

This is the Faraday disc generator formula. For mercury torus of inner radius r1,
outer radius r2, rotating at omega in field B_z:
  EMF_mercury = (1/2) * B_z * omega * (r2^2 - r1^2)

The radial current driven by this EMF through mercury's resistance:
  I_radial = EMF_mercury / R_torus
  R_torus = rho_Hg * ln(r2/r1) / (2 * pi * h)  [h = torus height]

Lorentz torque on mercury from its own induced current in B_z:
  tau_mercury = I_radial * B_z * (r2^2 - r1^2) / 2

This is the self-consistent Hartmann-flow type calculation for conducting fluid rotation
in an axial field. Whether this produces a net vertical force (anti-gravity) is the
unresolved question.

---

## 8. Vacuum Energy Density (Referenced Implicitly)

Zero-point energy density from QFT (relevant to Drew's "empty space" cosmology reference):
  rho_vacuum = (1/(2*pi^2)) * integral_0^{Lambda} (hbar * sqrt(k^2 + m^2)) * k^2 dk

For massless photons with UV cutoff at Planck scale Lambda_Pl = sqrt(hbar*c/G) ~ 1.22 x 10^19 GeV:
  rho_vacuum ~ Lambda_Pl^4 / (16 * pi^2) ~ 10^76 GeV/cm^3 ~ 10^114 J/m^3

Observed dark energy density:
  rho_Lambda_obs ~ 10^-29 g/cm^3 ~ 10^-9 J/m^3

Ratio:
  rho_vacuum / rho_Lambda_obs ~ 10^123

This 123-order-of-magnitude discrepancy (the cosmological constant problem) is the
"mystery" Drew points to when noting galaxies "arise from empty space." He does not
provide a resolution; he references it as motivation for studying "unseen forces."

---

## 9. Inertia, Magnetism, Gravity — Dimensional Connections Referenced

Drew's tweet 2044541150003110357 lists:
  "Inertia, electricity, magnetism, gravity, or even ships to fly magically through space"

In SI units, the fundamental electromagnetic-gravitational coupling constants:
  G (Newton) = 6.674 x 10^-11 N*m^2/kg^2
  epsilon_0 = 8.854 x 10^-12 F/m
  mu_0 = 4*pi*10^-7 H/m
  c = 1/sqrt(epsilon_0 * mu_0) = 2.998 x 10^8 m/s

The ratio of electromagnetic to gravitational force between two protons:
  F_EM / F_grav = e^2 / (4*pi*epsilon_0*G*m_p^2) ~ 1.24 x 10^36

This "hierarchy problem" (why gravity is 36 orders weaker than electromagnetism) is
implicitly referenced when Drew seeks electromagnetic mechanisms to overcome gravitational
acceleration.

# overall_Math.mdx
# All Mathematical Equations, Components, and Relationships

Source: Red Collie (Dr. Horace Drew), @RedCollie1
Extraction date: 2026-04-22

## 1. Capacitor Energy Storage and Discharge

Source: 13_1914664247965171712_preview.txt, 13_1914664288897392642_preview.txt

Capacitor stored energy:
    E = (1/2) * C * V^2

where:
* E = energy in joules (J)
* C = capacitance in farads (F)
* V = voltage at which capacitor is charged (V)

For N capacitors in parallel:
    C_parallel = N * C_individual
    E_total = (1/2) * N * C_individual * V^2

The three-capacitor bank observed (N = 3) triples the total available energy and capacitance.

Instantaneous discharge current (into load resistance R):
    I(t) = (V_0 / R) * exp(-t / (R * C))

Peak current at t=0:
    I_peak = V_0 / R

The time constant:
    tau_RC = R * C

For supercapacitors with C = 10 F, R = 0.1 ohm: tau = 1 s (slow discharge).
For electrolytic capacitors with C = 10^-2 F, R = 0.1 ohm: tau = 10^-3 s (pulse discharge).

---

## 2. Three-Phase Rotating Magnetic Field

Source: 13_2044596310473580544_video.mdx

Three-phase supply with phases separated by 2*pi/3 radians (120 degrees):
    I_1(t) = I_0 * cos(omega * t)
    I_2(t) = I_0 * cos(omega * t - 2*pi/3)
    I_3(t) = I_0 * cos(omega * t - 4*pi/3)

Magnetic field contributions from three coils at angles 0, 2*pi/3, 4*pi/3 in the XY-plane:
    B_x(t) = B_0 * [cos(0) * I_1(t) + cos(2*pi/3) * I_2(t) + cos(4*pi/3) * I_3(t)]
    B_y(t) = B_0 * [sin(0) * I_1(t) + sin(2*pi/3) * I_2(t) + sin(4*pi/3) * I_3(t)]

Evaluating using trigonometric identities:
    B_x(t) = (3/2) * B_0 * I_0 * cos(omega * t)
    B_y(t) = (3/2) * B_0 * I_0 * sin(omega * t)

The resultant field vector:
    B_rot(t) = (3/2) * B_0 * I_0 * [cos(omega * t) x-hat + sin(omega * t) y-hat]

Magnitude: |B_rot| = (3/2) * B_0 * I_0 = constant.
The field vector rotates uniformly in the XY-plane at angular frequency omega = 2*pi*f.

For f = 12 Hz (observed oscillation rate of disk magnet):
    omega = 2 * pi * 12 = 75.4 rad/s

The rotating field period: T = 1/f = 1/12 s ≈ 83 ms.

---

## 3. Magnetic Torque on Disk Magnet

Source: 13_2044596310473580544_video.mdx

Torque on a magnetic dipole m in external field B:
    tau = m x B

where m = M * V_magnet * n-hat (M = remanent magnetization of magnet, V_magnet = volume, n-hat = dipole axis unit vector).

For a disk magnet (diameter d = 50 mm, central bore diameter d_bore = 20 mm, thickness t):
    V_magnet = pi * t * [(d/2)^2 - (d_bore/2)^2] = pi * t * [(0.025)^2 - (0.010)^2] = pi * t * (6.25 - 1.00) x 10^-4 = pi * t * 5.25 x 10^-4 m^3

For NdFeB magnet with M ≈ 10^6 A/m:
    |m| = 10^6 * pi * t * 5.25 x 10^-4 = 1.65 * t (A*m^2) [where t is in meters]

Maximum torque when m is perpendicular to B:
    |tau_max| = |m| * |B|

This torque drives the magnet to align with the rotating field vector. If the moment of inertia of the disk magnet about its central axis is I_disk:
    I_disk = (1/2) * M_disk * [(r_outer)^2 - (r_inner)^2]

the angular acceleration at maximum torque:
    alpha = tau_max / I_disk

For large enough torque relative to I_disk, the magnet synchronizes with the rotating field (synchronous motor operation). At 12 Hz this is readily achievable for small disk magnets.

---

## 4. Counter-Rotating Frequency and Relative Angular Velocity

Source: 13_2044596310473580544_video.mdx

Inner magnet angular frequency: omega_c (clockwise, so -omega_c in standard convention)
Outer flywheel angular frequency: omega_f (anticlockwise, +omega_f)

Relative angular velocity between inner magnet and outer flywheel:
    omega_rel = omega_f + omega_c = omega_f - (-omega_c)

For omega_f = 2*pi*40 = 251.3 rad/s and omega_c = 2*pi*40 = 251.3 rad/s:
    omega_rel = 251.3 + 251.3 = 502.6 rad/s = 2*pi*80 rad/s → 80 Hz

This is the rate at which the relative phase between the two spinning magnetic assemblies changes. Any test object or measurement point in the inter-ring gap experiences a magnetic field pattern that cycles at 80 Hz.

---

## 5. Angular Momentum of Counter-Rotating Assembly

Source: 13_2044596310473580544_video.mdx, tweet 1957293340841709744

Angular momentum of flywheel:
    L_f = I_f * omega_f (anticlockwise)

Angular momentum of central magnet:
    L_c = I_c * omega_c (clockwise) = -I_c * omega_c (in same sign convention)

Net angular momentum:
    L_net = I_f * omega_f - I_c * omega_c

In the limit I_f * omega_f = I_c * omega_c:
    L_net = 0

A system with L_net = 0 has no gyroscopic resistance to precession (it behaves as if it were not spinning, from the perspective of external torques). This cancellation of angular momenta in the counter-rotating assembly may be a key design feature of the proposed drive — it would allow the spin axis to reorient without the gyroscopic resistance typical of a single fast-spinning rotor.

---

## 6. Dipole-Dipole Magnetic Interaction Force

Source: 13_2044596310473580544_video.mdx, overall magnetic framework

Force between two aligned magnetic dipoles m_1 and m_2 separated by distance r along the axis:
    F_axial = (3 * mu_0 / (2 * pi)) * m_1 * m_2 / r^4

(attractive for aligned dipoles, repulsive for antiparallel)

Force on central magnet (south pole up) from four surrounding ring magnets (north pole up), at a common height (r = horizontal ring radius):
The central magnet is attracted in all four horizontal directions, but these cancel by symmetry. The net force is axial.

If the central magnet is displaced upward by delta_z from the plane of the ring magnets, the force from each ring magnet has a downward component (restoring toward the ring plane). This creates a stable equilibrium in the axial direction at the ring plane — which is consistent with the observed "hovering right at the same level as those ring magnets because it's attracted to it at all four sides."

When three-phase drive causes the central magnet to jump upward above the ring plane, it encounters a repulsive region (if above the north-pole-up ring magnets, the south-pole-up central magnet is now approaching the south poles of the ring magnets from above — net repulsion). This creates the "barrier of attraction" described: "upward jumping force from below the plane to the plane where it hits a barrier of attraction."

---

## 7. Gyroscope Precession Rate

Source: 13_1957293251477811200_video.mdx

Standard gyroscope precession angular velocity:
    Omega_p = tau / L = (M * g * r_cm) / (I * omega)

where:
* Omega_p = precession rate (rad/s)
* tau = gravitational torque = M * g * r_cm (N*m)
* M = gyroscope mass (kg)
* g = gravitational acceleration = 9.81 m/s^2
* r_cm = distance from pivot to center of mass (m)
* I = moment of inertia about spin axis (kg*m^2)
* omega = spin angular velocity (rad/s)

For a lopsided gyroscope with additional mass m_tack at distance r_tack from spin axis:
    tau_additional = m_tack * g * r_tack * sin(theta)

where theta is the angle between the spin axis and vertical. The precession goes clockwise (viewed from above) for a gyroscope with its angular momentum pointing upward and the gravitational torque pointing in the horizontal plane away from the center-of-mass displacement.

Drew's "vortex theory" is a phenomenological re-description: the precession is said to occur because "there's a vortex in space created by the spinning gyroscope" and "it's pressing against normal space and rolling with it like that just sideways." This is not a mathematically distinct prediction from the standard formula above — it is a different physical picture that leads to the same observed precession direction and rate.

---

## 8. Topological Mathematical Content — Celtic Knot as Torus Knot

Source: 3_1923179966268841984.txt (image description of crop circle)

From the image description of the crop circle at The Gallops, Wiltshire, 15 May 2025:
"Celtic quaternary knots represent continuous looping with no beginning or end — a topological motif. In the context of UAP physics and crop circle research, the Celtic knot is sometimes cited as an ancient representation of: (1) topological field structures (field lines that continuously loop), (2) torus knots (mathematical knots that live on the surface of a torus), or (3) the Hopf fibration."

Mathematical content cited:

Torus knot T(p,q): A torus knot lives on the surface of a torus T^2 = S^1 x S^1 in R^3. It winds p times around the longitudinal direction and q times around the meridional direction. The quaternary (4-fold symmetry) Celtic knot in this formation is consistent with T(4,2) or T(2,4) topology (an unknot) or T(4,3) (a proper knot).

Hopf fibration: The Hopf fibration is a continuous surjection from S^3 to S^2 with fiber S^1:
    h: S^3 → S^2

Every point on S^2 has a preimage that is a circle (S^1) in S^3. The fibers are linked Hopf circles — each pair of fibers is linked exactly once. The Hopf fibration appears in quantum mechanics (spinor fibration), magnetic monopole theory (fiber bundle over S^2 with U(1) gauge structure), and topological field theory.

In the context of rotating magnetic fields: A rotating magnetic dipole field has a topological structure that can be related to the Hopf fibration through the hairy ball theorem and the classification of vector fields on S^2.

## 9. Rail Gun Acceleration Math

Source: 13_1914664288897392642_preview.txt

For a rail gun driven by capacitor bank, the equation of motion of the armature (mass m_armature) along the rails:
    m_armature * (d^2 x / dt^2) = F(t) = (1/2) * (dL/dx) * I(t)^2

where L(x) is the inductance as a function of armature position x, and I(t) is the discharge current.

The per-unit-length inductance gradient for parallel rails of separation w:
    dL/dx ≈ mu_0 / pi * [ln(w/r) + 0.25]

where r is the rail conductor radius.

For a simple LC discharge circuit (capacitor C discharging through rail inductance L and resistance R):
    L * (d^2 q / dt^2) + R * (dq / dt) + q/C = 0

where q is the charge remaining on the capacitor. This gives oscillatory (underdamped) or critically/overdamped discharge depending on the damping ratio:
    zeta = R / (2 * sqrt(L/C))

The muzzle energy is:
    E_muzzle = (1/2) * m_armature * v_final^2 = (1/2) * C * V_0^2 * eta

where eta is the efficiency (typically 1-40% for simple lab rail guns).

## 1. Capacitor Energy Storage and Pulse Current Delivery

From preview file 13_1914664288897392642_preview.txt (explicitly stated):

Energy stored in capacitor bank:
  E = (1/2) * C * V^2
For three capacitors in parallel: C_total = C_1 + C_2 + C_3

Instantaneous discharge current:
  I = C * (dV/dt)
For a resistive-inductive circuit discharge (RLC):
  I(t) = (V_0 / sqrt(L/C)) * exp(-R*t / (2L)) * sin(omega_0 * t)
  omega_0 = sqrt(1/(L*C) - (R/(2L))^2)

For the rail apparatus (inferred from description): three large capacitors
(~100-1000 microfarads at ~100-400 V) providing:
  E ~ (1/2) * (3 * C) * V^2 ~ (1/2) * (3 * 0.001 F) * (200 V)^2 = 60 J (order of magnitude estimate)
  Peak I ~ V_0 / sqrt(L/C) (depends on inductance of the rail circuit)

## 2. Relative Angular Velocity of Counter-Rotating Magnetic Elements

From video 13_2044596310473580544 and tweet 2044598282689941568:

Central magnet spin rate (proposed): omega_1 ~ 40 Hz (2.5 rad/s * Hz conversion: 40 Hz = 40 * 2*pi rad/s = 251 rad/s)
Flywheel counter-spin rate: omega_2 ~ 40 Hz (anticlockwise, i.e., -omega_1 direction)

Relative angular velocity:
  omega_rel = omega_1 + omega_2 = 40 + 40 = 80 Hz
(Because they rotate in opposite directions, relative velocity is the sum of magnitudes.)
  omega_rel_rad = 80 * 2*pi = 502.7 rad/s

At omega_2 = 20 Hz (moderate speed as stated in video):
  omega_rel = omega_1(~40) + omega_2(~20) = ~60 Hz

## 3. Gyroscopic Precession Rate (Standard Classical Derivation)

Standard result for precession angular velocity under gravitational torque:
  Omega_p = (M * g * r) / L = (M * g * r) / (I * omega)
where:
  M = mass of gyroscope
  g = 9.81 m/s^2 (gravitational acceleration)
  r = distance from pivot to center of mass
  I = principal moment of inertia about spin axis
  omega = spin angular velocity (rad/s)

Direction: Omega_p is perpendicular to L (angular momentum), causing L to precess around
the vertical (gravity direction). For standard spin orientation (upward angular momentum
vector, gravitational torque pointing horizontally), precession is clockwise viewed from above.

The experiment in video 13_1957293251477811200 adds an asymmetric mass ("blue tackle") to
one side, increasing the gravitational torque tau = r x (M_added * g) on the loaded side,
which increases Omega_p locally and causes the gyroscope to drift in one direction.

---

## 4. Lorentz Force in Homopolar / Liquid-Metal Motor

Standard expression:
  F = q * (v x B) (for a charge carrier)
  f = J x B (force per unit volume, for current density J in field B)
  tau = integral(r x (J x B)) dV (net torque on conducting body)

For radial current flow (J = J_r * r_hat) in axial field (B = B_z * z_hat):
  J x B = (J_r * B_z) * (r_hat x z_hat) = J_r * B_z * (-theta_hat)
(The azimuthal force is in the -theta direction for outward radial current in upward B.)
Net torque drives the conductor in the azimuthal direction (spin).

Applied to galinstan vortex:
  tau_azimuthal = (J_r * B_z) * Volume_active
  Power_input = tau * omega = I * V (energy conservation in ideal motor)

At 12V DC: P = V * I. Wire heating P_heat = I^2 * R_wire.
Fraction wasted as heat: eta = 1 - R_wire / R_total. For low-resistance galinstan:
R_galinstan << R_wire => most power is dissipated in the wire, not the motor.
Engineering solution: add series resistance R_s or use thicker/lower-resistance wire.

---

## 5. Axial Oscillation Drive Frequency and Magnet Parameters

From video 13_2044596310473580544:
* 50 mm diameter disk magnet, 20 mm center hole: oscillates at ~12 Hz under three-phase
  drive. At higher frequency (e.g., ~40-50 Hz), magnet rise is observed.
* 60 mm diameter, 20 mm hole: off-axis wobble at low power; upward jump at increased
  power; downward displacement at high power (goes below the ring plane).

The axial resonance frequency of the disk magnet in the potential well of the ring magnets
depends on:
  omega_resonance = sqrt(k_eff / m)
where:
  k_eff = -d^2U/dz^2 (effective axial spring constant from magnetic potential energy landscape)
  m = disk magnet mass

The observation of periodic up-down oscillation at 12 Hz for the 50 mm magnet may
correspond to the natural axial resonance frequency of that magnet in the ring potential.

---

## 6. Three-Phase Rotating Field Vector (Mathematical Description)

For a three-phase AC supply with angular frequency omega and phase separation 2*pi/3:
  B_1(t) = B_0 * cos(omega * t) * n_hat_1
  B_2(t) = B_0 * cos(omega * t - 2*pi/3) * n_hat_2
  B_3(t) = B_0 * cos(omega * t - 4*pi/3) * n_hat_3
where n_hat_1, n_hat_2, n_hat_3 are unit vectors in the stator plane at 120-degree intervals.

The vector sum:
  B_total(t) = (3/2) * B_0 * [cos(omega*t) * x_hat + sin(omega*t) * y_hat]
This is a rotating field of constant magnitude (3/2)*B_0 at angular frequency omega.
Source: six-wire coil assembly ("six wire coils" mentioned in video 13_2044596310473580544).

Ring magnet counter-spin drive: "Actually they're using clockwise three phase power to do
so for these six wire coils." This means the three-phase supply phase sequence drives the
ring magnets in the clockwise direction, while the crop-picture prescription calls for
counter-clockwise ring rotation — achieved by reversing two of the three phase connections
(phase reversal in a three-phase system reverses the rotation direction of the rotating field).

---

## 7. Scale Weight Measurement Equation for Anomalous Lift Detection

Proposed experiment from video 13_2044596310473580544:
Total system weight measurement on scale:
  W_measured = W_true - F_lift_anomalous
where F_lift_anomalous is any non-Newtonian upward force generated by the counter-rotating
magnetic system.

Standard prediction: F_lift_anomalous = 0 (Newton's Third Law holds, internal forces cancel).
Claimed possibility: F_lift_anomalous > 0 at omega_rel = 80 Hz.

If W_measured < W_true (static weight), this constitutes evidence for anomalous lift.
The measurement requires accurate baseline (device off) vs. active (device spinning at
omega_1 + omega_2 ~ 80 Hz relative) comparison.
Thermal drift and vibration are confounds requiring careful experimental design.

# overall_Math.mdx
# All Mathematical Equations, Their Components, and Relationships
# Source: RedCollie1 (Dr. Horace Drew) tweets, batch 7/10

---

## A. Vortex Physics Formula (Claimed)

### Formula
  ω = h / a

### Components
  ω: angular frequency of the spinning vortex (rad/s)
  h: height of the spinning vortex (m)
  a: cross-sectional area of the vortex = π × R² (m²)
  R: radius of the vortex (m)

### Derived Forms
  ω = h / (π × R²)
  h = ω × π × R²
  R = sqrt(h / (ω × π))

### Relationships Described
* Increasing ω (faster spin) at fixed R → larger h (taller vortex)
* Increasing R (wider vortex) at fixed ω → smaller h (shorter vortex)
* Increasing h (taller desired vortex) at fixed R → requires larger ω

### Dimensional Analysis
Standard SI:
  [ω] = s⁻¹
  [h/a] = m / m² = m⁻¹

These dimensions do not match. The formula as stated requires either:
  (a) a proportionality constant k with units [k] = m·s⁻¹: ω = k × h / a
  (b) h is not in meters but in some angular or frequency unit
  (c) The formula is an empirical scaling relation with unstated units convention

The formula is presented as received (claimed dream / psychic message) and described as
"transitional magnetism" governing UFO vortex physics. It is not derived from first principles
in the source material.
Source: YAML 1957348224119017742, note_tweet.

---

## B. Homopolar Generator EMF

### Standard Formula (Faraday Disc)
  EMF = (1/2) × B × ω × (R_outer² - R_inner²)

### Components
  B: axial magnetic field through the disc (T)
  ω: angular velocity of disc (rad/s)
  R_outer: outer radius of disc (m)
  R_inner: inner (hub) radius of disc (m)

### Derivation sketch
The EMF is derived by integrating the motional EMF (Lorentz force on charges) along a radial path:
  EMF = ∫[R_inner to R_outer] (v × B) · dr = ∫[R_inner to R_outer] (ω × r × B) dr
       = ω × B × ∫[R_inner to R_outer] r dr = ω × B × (R_outer² - R_inner²) / 2

### Applied to Paulsen Disc (12-Magnet Periphery)
For the Paulsen disc, B is not uniform — it is provided by 12 peripheral permanent magnets
(6N + 6S at 30° spacing). The effective B for EMF calculation is:

  B_eff = (1/πR²) × ∫∫ B_z(r,φ) dA

the area-averaged axial field over the disc face. For alternating polarity peripheral magnets,
the net flux through the disc may be significantly less than the peak pole field.

### Two Counter-Rotating Discs
For two discs rotating at ±ω:
  EMF₁ = (1/2) × B_eff × ω × (R₂² - R₁²)  [disc 1, CW]
  EMF₂ = (1/2) × B_eff × ω × (R₂² - R₁²)  [disc 2, CCW — same sign due to both ω and
                                               effective B_eff sign reversing together]
Total output if hubs connected in series:
  EMF_total = EMF₁ + EMF₂ = B_eff × ω × (R₂² - R₁²)

Source: TXT 3_1914665447687118849; YAML 1914669302005027316, note_tweet.

---

## C. Gyroscopic Precession Rate

### Formula
  Ω = τ / L = τ / (I × ω_spin)

### Components
  Ω: precession angular velocity (rad/s)
  τ: applied torque (N·m)
  L: angular momentum = I × ω_spin (kg·m²/s)
  I: moment of inertia of spinning magnet about spin axis (kg·m²)
  ω_spin: spin angular velocity (rad/s)

For a disc magnet (solid cylinder approximation):
  I = (1/2) × m × r²
where m is disc mass and r is disc radius.

For the 70 mm diameter disc magnet (r = 35 mm = 0.035 m):
  I = (1/2) × m × (0.035)² = (1/2) × m × 1.225 × 10⁻³ m²
  I ≈ 6.1 × 10⁻⁴ × m [kg·m²] for mass m in kg

Applied torque from three-phase rotating field on the precessing magnet:
  τ = m_magnetic × B × sin(α)
where m_magnetic is the magnetic dipole moment of the disc (A·m²), B is the field amplitude,
and α is the angle between the magnetic moment and the field.

At resonance (spin frequency = field frequency), α → 0, τ → 0, and precession rate decreases.
The rise behavior at high rpm is argued to occur near or above this resonance condition.

## D. Euler's Equations for Symmetric Top Under Three-Phase Torque

### Euler's Equations
  I_⊥ × (dω₁/dt) + (I_∥ - I_⊥) × ω₂ × ω₃ = τ₁
  I_⊥ × (dω₂/dt) + (I_⊥ - I_∥) × ω₁ × ω₃ = τ₂
  I_∥ × (dω₃/dt) = τ₃

### Under Three-Phase Rotating Torque
  τ₁(t) = τ₀ × cos(ω_s × t)
  τ₂(t) = τ₀ × sin(ω_s × t)
  τ₃(t) = 0

This drives forced nutation. At resonance ω_s = Ω_nutation (natural nutation frequency):
  Ω_nutation = I_∥ × ω_spin / I_⊥

the response amplitude grows, leading to large-angle precession and potentially the rising
behavior observed.

### Setup
Permanent magnet with dipole moment m = m_z ẑ placed in rotating field:
  B(t) = B₀ × [cos(ω_s t) x̂ + sin(ω_s t) ŷ]

### Torque
  τ = m × B = m_z ẑ × B₀ [cos(ω_s t) x̂ + sin(ω_s t) ŷ]
  τ = m_z × B₀ [cos(ω_s t) (ẑ × x̂) + sin(ω_s t) (ẑ × ŷ)]
  τ = m_z × B₀ [cos(ω_s t) ŷ - sin(ω_s t) x̂]

This torque lies in the XY-plane and oscillates. For the Z-aligned dipole, there is no net

Each coil i produces a field contribution along its axis:

Summing all three:

This is a field of constant amplitude (3/2)B₀I₀ rotating at angular frequency ω_s.

The Corbino effect is most pronounced at large Hall angles (semiconducting or high-field regime).

## 1. Homopolar Generator EMF — Exact Derivation

EMF = ∫₀ᴿ (v × B) · dr

Vector components:
* v = ωr φ̂  (velocity of disc element at radius r, angular velocity ω)
* B = B_z ẑ  (uniform axial magnetic field)

Cross product: v × B = ωr(φ̂ × ẑ) = ωr(-r̂) = -ωr r̂

Dot with dr = dr r̂:
(v × B) · dr r̂ = -ωr B_z dr

Integrating outward (center to rim):
EMF = -∫₀ᴿ ωr B_z dr = -½ ω B_z R²

Magnitude: |EMF| = ½ ω B_z R²

Where:
* ω [rad/s] = angular velocity of conducting disc
* B_z [T] = axial component of magnetic flux density
* R [m] = disc radius
* EMF [V] = open-circuit voltage between center and rim

Key relationship: EMF ∝ ω × B_z × R² — quadratic in disc radius, linear in field strength
and rotation rate. Doubling R quadruples EMF; doubling ω or B_z doubles EMF.

---

## 2. Azimuthal Torque on Homopolar Motor Disc

Current I flows radially through disc cross-section from center (brush contact) to rim
(second brush contact):

Elemental force: dF = I (dL × B) = I (dr r̂ × B_z ẑ) = I B_z dr (r̂ × ẑ) = -I B_z dr φ̂

Elemental torque about z-axis: dτ = r × dF = r(-I B_z dr) = -r I B_z dr ẑ

Wait — torque magnitude per unit length element:
dτ_z = r |dF_φ| = r × I B_z dr

Total torque: τ_z = ∫₀ᴿ r I B_z dr = I B_z R²/2

Where:
* I [A] = radial current
* B_z [T] = axial field
* R [m] = disc radius
* τ_z [N·m] = torque about z-axis

Note: τ_z = EMF × I = P_mech / ω, consistent with energy conservation.

## 3. Three-Phase Rotating Magnetic Field — Phasor Analysis

Three coils (a, b, c) at spatial positions 0°, 120°, 240° in the XY-plane.
Coil a produces field: B_a(t) = B_max cos(ωt) x̂
Coil b produces field: B_b(t) = B_max cos(ωt - 2π/3)(−½x̂ + (√3/2)ŷ)
Coil c produces field: B_c(t) = B_max cos(ωt + 2π/3)(−½x̂ − (√3/2)ŷ)

Total field:
B_x(t) = B_max[cos(ωt) - ½cos(ωt-2π/3) - ½cos(ωt+2π/3)]
       = B_max[cos(ωt) - ½·2cos(ωt)cos(2π/3)]
       = B_max[cos(ωt) + ½cos(ωt)]  [since cos(2π/3) = -½]
       = (3/2)B_max cos(ωt)

B_y(t) = B_max[(√3/2)cos(ωt-2π/3) - (√3/2)cos(ωt+2π/3)]
       = B_max(√3/2)[2sin(ωt)sin(2π/3)]
       = B_max(√3/2)(√3)sin(ωt)
       = (3/2)B_max sin(ωt)

Result: B_total(t) = (3/2)B_max [cos(ωt) x̂ + sin(ωt) ŷ]

This is a vector of constant magnitude (3/2)B_max rotating at angular frequency ω in the
XY-plane. The factor 3/2 is the three-phase RMF amplitude gain (larger than any single
coil's B_max by 50%).

## 4. Five-Phase Rotating Magnetic Field

For 5 coils at 72° spacing, phase offset 2π/5 per coil:
I_k(t) = I_0 cos(ωt - 2π(k-1)/5), k = 1,...,5
Coil k is at angular position θ_k = 2π(k-1)/5.

MMF contribution from coil k at angle θ:
F_k(θ,t) = N I_k(t) cos(θ - θ_k)

Total MMF:
F(θ,t) = N I_0 Σ_{k=1}^{5} cos(ωt - 2πk/5) cos(θ - 2πk/5)

Using product-to-sum: cos(A)cos(B) = ½[cos(A-B) + cos(A+B)]

F(θ,t) = (5/2)N I_0 cos(θ - ωt) + (harmonics at ±5 spatial frequency)

Fundamental component: (5/2)N I_0 cos(θ - ωt) — a traveling wave rotating at ω.
Lowest significant space harmonic: 5th harmonic (vs. 3rd in 3-phase).

This means a 5-phase RMF has lower harmonic torque ripple than 3-phase, but requires 5
independent power phases. Drew's association: the 5 "moon" shapes (coils) on the Buga orb
exterior correspond to a 5-phase stator producing this smoother RMF.

Two magnetic dipoles m_1, m_2 aligned anti-parallel (same N-pole toward each other)
on the z-axis at separation z:

This is repulsive (positive, upward on upper dipole when both oriented north-up).

U = -(μ_0 / 4π) × (m_1 · m_2) / z³ × (2 - 3sin²θ)

For two co-axial counter-rotating discs:

* Red outer flywheel: moment of inertia I_r, angular velocity -Ω_r → L_r = -I_r Ω_r ẑ

## 8. MHD Hartmann Number for Mercury Spinning in Magnetic Field

Ha = B × a × (σ / η)^(1/2)

Where:
* B [T] = applied magnetic field strength
* a [m] = characteristic length (container radius)
* σ [S/m] = electrical conductivity of fluid
* η [Pa·s] = dynamic viscosity of fluid

Mercury (Hg at 25°C):
* σ_Hg = 1.044 × 10^6 S/m
* η_Hg = 1.526 × 10^-3 Pa·s

For B = 0.1 T, a = 0.05 m:
Ha = 0.1 × 0.05 × (1.044×10^6 / 1.526×10^-3)^(1/2)
   = 0.005 × (6.84×10^8)^(1/2)
   = 0.005 × 2.615×10^4
   ≈ 131

Ha >> 1: flow in the bulk of the fluid is dominated by electromagnetic body forces
rather than viscous forces. Hartmann boundary layers of thickness δ ~ a/Ha ≈ 0.38 mm
form at the walls.

Galinstan (Ga-In-Sn eutectic, liquid at room temperature):
* σ_galinstan ≈ 3.46 × 10^6 S/m
* η_galinstan ≈ 2 × 10^-3 Pa·s

For same B, a:
Ha_galinstan = 0.005 × (3.46×10^6 / 2×10^-3)^(1/2)
             = 0.005 × (1.73×10^9)^(1/2)
             = 0.005 × 4.16×10^4
             ≈ 208

Even higher Ha — stronger MHD coupling for galinstan than mercury at same conditions.

## Appended Content — Additional Mathematics from Full Source Review (2026-04-22)

### 11. Lorentz Force on Spinning Magnetic Dipole in Rotating Magnetic Field

For a magnetic dipole m = m_0 ẑ (north-up) spinning at angular velocity ω_m in a rotating field B_RMF rotating at ω_stator:

The interaction energy: U(t) = -m · B_RMF(t)

For m and B_RMF coaxial and co-rotating at the same speed (synchronous): U is constant, producing sustained torque rather than oscillating torque.

The synchronous torque (per classical induction theory):
τ = m × B_RMF = |m||B_RMF| sin(δ) φ̂

where δ is the phase lag between the rotor dipole axis and the RMF vector. At δ = 90°, torque is maximum. At δ = 0°, torque is zero but the rotor is in stable equilibrium (analogous to synchronous motor operation at rated load).

For the Z-axis force (not predicted by classical induction theory):
If the RMF has a Z-axis gradient component dB_z/dz ≠ 0, the axial force on the dipole is:
F_z = m_z (∂B_z/∂z) + m_x (∂B_x/∂z) + m_y (∂B_y/∂z)

In the time-average over one RMF rotation cycle, the m_x and m_y terms average to zero for a rotor spinning synchronously. Only the m_z term survives:
<F_z> = m_z <∂B_z/∂z>

This is classical magnetic gradient levitation. The stator's fringe field above the coil plane has a negative dB_z/dz (field decreases with height), giving: <F_z> = m_z × (negative gradient) — downward if m_z is positive (north-up). This cannot levitate a north-up rotor by this mechanism alone.

Drew's implied alternative: the spinning rotor in the counter-spin configuration generates an additional field that modifies dB_z/dz at the rotor location, changing the sign of the gradient force. This is the non-classical element and the one requiring experimental verification.

### 12. Synchronous Speed and Slip in Context of Levitation

For a p-pole-pair motor driven at electrical frequency f_e:
n_s = 60 f_e / p [RPM]

Slip: s = (n_s - n_rotor) / n_s

At slip = 0 (synchronous): rotor spins at exactly the RMF speed. No torque for induction (asynchronous) motor; finite torque for synchronous motor.

For Drew's levitation cases:
* 3-phase, 6 Hz, n_c = 6 coils, p = 3 (6 magnets / 2): n_s = 60 × 6 / 3 = 120 RPM
* 3-phase, 6 Hz, n_c = 6 coils, p = 2 (4 magnets): n_s = 60 × 6 / 2 = 180 RPM
* 3-phase, 6 Hz, n_c = 6 coils, p = 1.5 (3 magnets) — non-integer pole pairs: this is the unusual "3 magnets over 6 coils" configuration where classical theory predicts poor coupling.

The 3-magnet case with 6 coils is mathematically the most anomalous: 3 magnets create a 3-pole (p = 3/2, non-integer pole pair) configuration with respect to the 6-coil stator. Classical analysis predicts no synchronous coupling for non-integer p. Yet Drew reports levitation. This is the strongest departure from classical motor theory in his reported results.

### 13. Pi Encoding in Barbury Castle Crop Picture — Rotary Decimal Encoding

Tweet 2000689570321678421: π ≈ 3.141592654 encoded in a crop picture at Barbury Castle, June 1, 2008.

The proposed rotary encoding scheme: consider a full circle (2π radians or 360°) divided into angular sectors. If the circle is divided into 10 equal sectors (each 36°) and each sector is labeled with a digit 0-9, then a sequence of angular markers at positions 3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6, 5, 4 (reading digits of π from left to right) would encode π.

Alternatively: the crop picture uses a logarithmic spiral or radial segment pattern where the number of cells or nodes at each radial position encodes successive decimal digits. A "rotary code for 3.14" in the follow-up picture is consistent with a 3-armed spiral with angular markers. The mathematical constant being encoded is standard; the claim is that the pattern has an angular precision inconsistent with manual agricultural flattening.

Precision required: to encode π to 10 digits (±0.0000000005), the angular positions of crop features would need to be accurate to about 1/10^9 of a full circle — less than 0.000001°. Actual crop features have angular precision of perhaps 0.1° at best. Therefore the "encoding" must be at the level of discrete cell counts (integers) rather than analog angular positions, in which case encoding π to 10 digits requires at least 10 discrete counting events, each correctly resolved. Whether the crop picture structure actually does this consistently is an empirical question about the pattern analysis.

## 1. Homopolar Generator EMF

From context of tweet 1914936648145555818 (Faraday's Paradox for homopolar motor/generator):

EMF = (1/2) ω B r²

Components:
* ω = angular velocity of the rotating conducting disc [rad/s]
* B = axial magnetic flux density at the disc [T]
* r = radius of the conducting disc [m]
* EMF = open-circuit electromotive force [V]

This arises from integrating the motional EMF (v × B) along a radial path from axle to rim:

EMF = ∫₀ʳ (v × B) · dr̂ dr = ∫₀ʳ (ω r B) dr = (1/2) ω B r²

where v = ω r φ̂ (azimuthal velocity) and B = B ẑ, so v × B = ω r B (φ̂ × ẑ) = ω r B (-r̂) — pointing radially inward, driving conventional current inward (from rim to axle) if ω and B are both positive by the right-hand convention.

Significance: this formula holds whether or not the magnet co-rotates with the disc. The resolution of Faraday's paradox claimed by the experimenter concerns precisely the reference-frame analysis of this result when the magnet rotates.

## 2. Lenz's Law — Faraday Induction

From note_tweet 1970030336232026143:

Faraday's law (differential form):

∇ × E = -∂B/∂t

For a conducting aluminum disc with conductivity σ in a time-varying applied field B_app(t):

J_eddy = σ E = -σ ∂A/∂t (in the Coulomb gauge, where A is the magnetic vector potential)

The induced eddy current density J_eddy creates a secondary magnetic field:

B_induced = ∇ × A_induced

By Lenz's law, B_induced opposes B_app:

B_induced · B_app < 0

The repulsive force between the induced field and the applied field:

F_repulsion = ∇(m_induced · B_app)

where m_induced is the effective magnetic dipole moment of the eddy current distribution:

m_induced = (1/2) ∫_V r × J_eddy dV

Since m_induced is anti-parallel to B_app, F_repulsion is directed away from the coil (upward, along -∇|B_app|).

## 3. Corbino Disc — Lorentz Force and Torque

From note_tweet 1992007523407466702:

Current density in Corbino disc (radial current drive):

J = J_r r̂

Applied axial field:

B = B_z ẑ

Lorentz body force density:

f = J × B = J_r r̂ × B_z ẑ = J_r B_z (r̂ × ẑ)

Using r̂ × ẑ = -φ̂:

f = -J_r B_z φ̂

Total azimuthal torque on annular disc element at radius r, thickness dz, width dr:

dτ = r × f · dV = r · (-J_r B_z) (2π r dr dz)

Integrated torque:

τ = -2π B_z J_r ∫_{r₁}^{r₂} ∫_0^t r² dr dz = -2π B_z J_r t (r₂³ - r₁³)/3

where t is the disc thickness, r₁ and r₂ are inner and outer radii.

For reversal via capacitor phase shift:

Time-averaged torque with AC fields B_z(t) = B_0 cos(ωt) and J_r(t) = J_0 cos(ωt + φ):

<τ> ∝ <J_r(t) B_z(t)> = (J_0 B_0 / 2) cos(φ)

At φ = π (180° phase shift from capacitive resonance above the driving frequency):

<τ> ∝ cos(π) = -1

Torque reverses sign — disc spins in the opposite direction.

## 4. Time-Averaged Weight — Periodic Rise/Fall Model

From note_tweet 1927593867060093435:

Let:
* W_0 = static weight of spinning magnet [g]
* f = fraction of cycle spent in free fall (downward phase)
* (1-f) = fraction of cycle in rising (upward-driven) phase

During free fall: effective weight on scale W_ff = 0
During rise: effective weight on scale W_rise ≈ W_0

Time-averaged apparent weight:

<W> = (1-f) · W_0 + f · 0 = (1-f) · W_0

For f = 0.5 (equal rise and fall time):

<W> = 0.5 · W_0

Numerical example given: W_0 = 100 g → <W> = 50 g (50% reduction).

## 5. Rotating Magnetic Field — Phase Vector Decomposition

For a symmetric n-phase AC supply with phases k = 0, 1, ..., n-1, each carrying current:

I_k(t) = I_0 cos(ωt - 2πk/n)

and coils arranged at azimuthal angles θ_k = 2πk/n:

The net magnetic field vector in the XY-plane:

B_xy(t) = B_0 Σ_k cos(ωt - 2πk/n) [cos(θ_k) x̂ + sin(θ_k) ŷ]

= B_0 (n/2) [cos(ωt) x̂ + sin(ωt) ŷ] (for n ≥ 3)

This is a uniformly rotating field of constant amplitude B_0 n/2, rotating at angular frequency ω. The amplitude does not pulsate (no torque ripple in the limit of continuous phases); for finite n, residual torque ripple decays rapidly with increasing n.

For n=3: B_xy(t) = (3/2)B_0 [cos(ωt) x̂ + sin(ωt) ŷ] — rotating field, amplitude = (3/2)B_0.
For n=5: B_xy(t) = (5/2)B_0 [cos(ωt) x̂ + sin(ωt) ŷ] — rotating field, amplitude = (5/2)B_0.

The Buga orb's 5-phase system produces 5/3 = 1.67× stronger rotating field amplitude than the 3-phase lab setup (for equal current and coil geometry), contributing to greater levitation force.

## 6. Axial Force on Spinning Magnet in Rotating Field — Dimensional Analysis

From video transcript (70 mm magnet, 20-30 Hz spin):

Upward force measured: F_up ≈ 500 g = 4.9 N

No formal derivation of F_up is given in the source material. However, the relevant parameters are:
* Permanent magnet dipole moment: m [A·m²]
* Rotating field amplitude: B_rot [T]
* Spin rate: ω_spin [rad/s]
* Axial field gradient: ∂B_z/∂z [T/m]

Standard magneto-mechanical force on a dipole in a non-uniform field:

F_z = m · ∂B_z/∂z

For a spinning magnet in a rotating field, the effective axial component of m that couples to the axial gradient varies with spin rate — higher ω_spin → stronger coupling of the rotating dipole to the axial gradient of the field envelope. This is qualitatively consistent with the observation that higher spin rates produce greater upward force.

Observed: coil assembly rotates CCW when magnet rotates CW (free coil condition, video 13_1934191685191507968).

Conservation:

L_magnet + L_coil = L_external (from driving current)

If the external supply delivers angular momentum at rate τ_drive:

dL_magnet/dt = τ_drive - τ_reaction

dL_coil/dt = τ_reaction (reaction torque on coil)

In steady state:

ω_magnet · I_magnet = -ω_coil · I_coil (equal and opposite angular momenta for an isolated system)

where I_magnet and I_coil are moments of inertia. The coil assembly is much larger than the magnet, so ω_coil << ω_magnet in steady state — consistent with observation.

For n-phase rotating field drive, the torque ripple on the driven rotor (assuming linear coupling) contains harmonics at multiples of n:

The dominant ripple term is at frequency nω. For 3-phase (n=3): dominant ripple at 3ω. For 5-phase (n=5): dominant ripple at 5ω, with smaller amplitude (a_1 for 5-phase < a_1 for 3-phase). ## 1. Special Relativity in 4D Euclidean Space: Geometric Parameterization

### Core Substitution
  sin(θ) = v/c

This maps relativistic velocity v (0 ≤ v < c) to a geometric angle θ ∈ [0°, 90°).

### Derived Identities
  cos(θ) = √(1 - v²/c²) = 1/γ   where γ = Lorentz factor
  tan(θ) = v/√(c² - v²) = βγ    where β = v/c
  θ → 90° as v → c               (lightspeed limit as right-angle limit)

### Lorentz Factor in Geometric Form
  γ = 1/cos(θ)

### Relativistic Energy in Geometric Form
  E = γm₀c² = m₀c²/cos(θ)

### Relativistic Momentum in Geometric Form
  p = γm₀v = m₀c × (sin(θ)/cos(θ)) = m₀c × tan(θ)

### Energy-Momentum Relation in Geometric Form
  E² - (pc)² = (m₀c²)²
  Dividing by E²:
    1 - (pc/E)² = (m₀c²/E)²
    1 - sin²(θ) = cos²(θ)  ✓ (Pythagorean identity)

This shows the relativistic energy-momentum hyperbola maps exactly to the unit circle
in the (E/m₀c², pc/m₀c²) plane under the sin(θ) = v/c parameterization.

### de Broglie Equation Connection

de Broglie wavelength: λ = h/p
Phase velocity of matter wave: v_ph = ω/k = E/p = c²/v

In geometric form:
  v_ph = c²/v = c/(v/c) = c/sin(θ)

Group velocity of matter wave: v_g = dω/dk = v (particle velocity)
  v_g = c sin(θ)

The dispersion relation:
  ω² = (ck)² + (m₀c²/ħ)²

maps in Euclidean 4D to the same geometric circle as the SR energy-momentum relation.
Drew's claim: both theories are presentations of the same Euclidean 4D rotation by angle θ,
not two independent empirical theories.

### Wick Rotation Correspondence
Under Wick rotation t → iτ (Euclidean continuation), the boost rapidity φ defined by:
  tanh(φ) = v/c

becomes:
  φ → iθ  where  sin(θ) = v/c

This is the precise mathematical content of Drew's assertion. The Lorentz group SO(1,3)
becomes the Euclidean rotation group SO(4) under Wick continuation, and the boost angle
becomes a real rotation angle.

# overall_Math.mdx
# All Mathematical Equations, Their Components, and Relationships

Source: RedCollie1 (Dr. Horace Drew), X/Twitter posts, batch 8/4
Extracted: 2026-04-22

====

## Note on Mathematical Explicitness in Source Material

The source tweets contain physics claims and experimental observations, but few fully written-out mathematical equations. Where Drew states a physics principle, the relevant mathematical formalism is reconstructed here at PhD level from the stated physics, preserving exact correspondence to what is claimed without invention of content not present in the sources.

====

## Lorentz Force on a Spinning Magnetic Body

Drew claims: "Newton's 3rd Law does not apply to a spinning Lorentz force."
(Source: tweet 2007971400427110683)

The Lorentz force on a charge q moving with velocity v in electromagnetic fields E and B:

  F = q(E + v × B)

For a magnetized body (permanent magnet) spinning with angular velocity Ω in an applied field B_ext:

The velocity of a charge at position r within the body (in lab frame):
  v = Ω × r

The Lorentz force on this charge from B_ext:
  F_Lorentz = q(v × B_ext) = q((Ω × r) × B_ext)

Expanding the triple cross product:
  (Ω × r) × B_ext = Ω(r · B_ext) - B_ext(r · Ω)

When integrated over the entire spinning magnetized body (all charges), the net force on the body is:

  F_net = ∫ ρ_charge [(Ω × r) × B_ext] dV

where ρ_charge is the charge density. For a neutral body with equal positive and negative charges, many terms cancel. The net Lorentz force on a spinning neutral magnetic body in an external field is in general non-zero because the magnetization M = (1/V)∫(r × J) dV contributes a current distribution that interacts with B_ext.

For a magnetic dipole m = M V in an external field B:
  F = ∇(m · B)    [force on a magnetic dipole in a gradient field]
  τ = m × B       [torque on a magnetic dipole]

These are the standard equations. Drew's claim requires an additional Z-axis force term that is not derivable from these expressions in classical electrodynamics — it would require either:
  (a) A field momentum contribution: p_field = ε_0 ∫(E × B) dV ≠ 0 under rotation
  (b) A new force term arising from the spinning geometry

====

## Three-Phase Rotating Field Mathematics

Six coils arranged as UVW, UVW (three phases, two coils per phase, in a ring).

For phase U at angle φ_U = 0:
  B_U(t) = B_0 cos(ωt) [cos(0) x̂ + sin(0) ŷ] = B_0 cos(ωt) x̂

For phase V at angle φ_V = 2π/3:
  B_V(t) = B_0 cos(ωt - 2π/3) [cos(2π/3) x̂ + sin(2π/3) ŷ]

For phase W at angle φ_W = 4π/3:
  B_W(t) = B_0 cos(ωt - 4π/3) [cos(4π/3) x̂ + sin(4π/3) ŷ]

Summing all three:
  B_total(t) = (3/2) B_0 [cos(ωt) x̂ + sin(ωt) ŷ]

This is a field of constant magnitude (3/2)B_0 rotating at angular frequency ω in the XY-plane (horizontal plane). At ω = 2π × 40 rad/s (40 Hz) or ω = 2π × 50 rad/s (50 Hz):
  |B_total| = (3/2) B_0 = constant
  Phase: φ(t) = ωt (linear in time)

Note: with six coils in two UVW pairs at 60° spacing (not 120°), the resultant field magnitude is still constant but the calculation includes both pairs. The field rotates at the electrical frequency.

====

## Torque on the Spinning Permanent Magnet

Torque on the magnet's dipole moment m in the rotating field B_total:
  τ = m × B_total

If m makes angle θ with B_total:
  |τ| = m B_total sin(θ)

For sub-synchronous operation (induction motor analogy), the slip angle δ = θ is maintained by the back-EMF of the spinning magnet. The continuous torque drives:
  I α = τ - τ_friction

where I = moment of inertia of magnet and α = angular acceleration. At steady state (α = 0):
  τ = τ_friction = constant = m B_total sin(δ_steady)

This determines the slip angle at steady-state spin.

====

## Magnetic Force on the Spinning Magnet: Z-Axis Component

For a magnetic dipole in a non-uniform field (the coil ring is at finite distance below the magnet, so dB/dz ≠ 0):

  F_z = (m · ∇) B_z + m_x (∂B_z/∂x) + m_y (∂B_z/∂y) + m_z (∂B_z/∂z)

For a magnet with dipole moment primarily in the Z-direction (m = m_z ẑ) in the rotating XY-plane field:
  F_z = m_z (∂B_z/∂z)

If the rotating field B_total is entirely in the XY-plane at the coil location, then B_z = 0 at that plane, but dB_z/dz may be non-zero above or below the coils. For a ring of coils carrying current I_coil at height z = 0, the axial field component at height z above the coil plane is:

  B_z(0, z) = (μ_0 I_coil R²) / [2(R² + z²)^(3/2)]

where R = coil ring radius. The gradient:
  ∂B_z/∂z = -3μ_0 I_coil R² z / [2(R² + z²)^(5/2)]

This is the classical gradient term. For z > 0 (magnet above the coil), ∂B_z/∂z < 0, so if m_z > 0:
  F_z = m_z (∂B_z/∂z) < 0    [downward force for magnet above coils, dipole pointing up]

This is the conventional result: a magnetic dipole in a gradient field is attracted toward the stronger field — which for the coil arrangement means downward toward the coils, not upward away from them. For the magnet to rise, a mechanism beyond this simple gradient force is required.

Drew's claim is that spinning the magnet changes this result — i.e., the Lorentz force on the spinning charge distribution generates an additional Z-axis force not captured by F_z = m·∇B.

====

## Anti-Gravity Force Measurement Equations

From tweet 1934367052594397363 (referenced parent tweet):
  "Small and reproducible anti-gravity effects of 30 to 50 grams, yet much of the upward spinning force of 500 grams (for this small magnet at 20-30 Hertz)."

Force unit conversion (gram-force to Newtons):
  30 g-force = 0.030 kg × 9.81 m/s² = 0.294 N
  50 g-force = 0.050 kg × 9.81 m/s² = 0.490 N
  500 g-force = 0.500 kg × 9.81 m/s² = 4.91 N

Efficiency (net anti-gravity / total upward spinning force):
  η = F_net_antigravity / F_total_upward = (30 to 50 g) / 500 g = 6% to 10%

This leaves 90-94% of the upward spinning force unaccounted for as net lift — dissipated as heat (eddy currents, hysteresis losses), friction, or canceled by stator reaction forces. The path to scaling up the device requires either (a) increasing efficiency to where F_net > mass of device, or (b) adding the homopolar dynamo reaction cancellation to recover the cancelled 90-94%.

====

## Homopolar Dynamo EMF Equation

Faraday/homopolar dynamo EMF:
  ε = (1/2) ω B r²

where:
  ε = electromotive force [V]
  ω = angular velocity of the conducting disc [rad/s]
  B = axial magnetic field threading the disc [T]
  r = radius of the disc [m]

For a self-exciting dynamo, the current generated by ε drives the coil that produces B:
  I = ε / R_circuit = ω B r² / (2 R_circuit)

The self-sustaining condition requires:
  B = μ_0 N I / L_coil    [Ampere's law for the coil]
  I = ω B r² / (2 R_circuit)    [Ohm's law + Faraday EMF]

Combining:
  B = μ_0 N ω B r² / (2 R_circuit L_coil)

Self-sustaining condition (critical angular velocity):
  1 = μ_0 N ω r² / (2 R_circuit L_coil)
  ω_c = 2 R_circuit L_coil / (μ_0 N r²)

For ω > ω_c, the dynamo is self-sustaining. For ω < ω_c, the field decays to zero and the dynamo dies. The liquid-metal (galinstan) dynamo must spin above ω_c for Drew's reaction-cancellation mechanism to function.

Galinstan properties relevant to this calculation:
  Electrical resistivity: ρ_galinstan ≈ 2.9 × 10^-7 Ω·m (at room temperature)
  This sets R_circuit ∝ ρ_galinstan × geometry.

For galinstan (density ≈ 6440 kg/m³), the viscous drag on the spinning liquid-metal disc sets a lower bound on the drive power needed to maintain ω > ω_c.

====

## Dual-Counter-Rotating Flywheel Angular Momentum

Inner flywheel (clockwise, angular velocity +ω_inner):
  L_inner = I_inner ω_inner ẑ

Outer flywheel (anticlockwise, angular velocity -ω_outer):
  L_outer = -I_outer ω_outer ẑ

Total angular momentum:
  L_total = (I_inner ω_inner - I_outer ω_outer) ẑ

For L_total = 0 (no net angular momentum, device does not precess):
  I_inner ω_inner = I_outer ω_outer

This is the design condition for a non-precessing levitation device. Drew's outer flywheel has larger magnets (30 mm vs. the inner's smaller magnets if 16 are used) and larger radius, so I_outer > I_inner. For balance, ω_outer < ω_inner — the outer flywheel must spin slower than the inner.

The 8 inner magnets and 8 outer magnets, driven by 6 three-phase coils arranged as UVW UVW, produce a slip frequency:
  f_slip = f_rotating_field - f_magnet_rotation
  τ ∝ sin(2π f_slip t)

The geometry of 8 magnets in a ring (8-fold symmetry) interacting with 6-coil 3-phase field (6-fold symmetry) produces a beating pattern at the least-common-multiple frequency, which could produce pulsed torque rather than constant torque — a detail that would affect smooth vs. pulsed levitation.

====

## Magnet Count: Allowed Combinations

Drew states: "eight magnets in each flywheel" for six coils; "12 or 24 magnets for nine coils."

The pattern: number of magnets must be a multiple of the number of coil pairs (i.e., a multiple of the phase number × 2 for a 3-phase system). For 6 coils (3-phase, 2 coils/phase): multiples of 2 × (something that divides evenly into 6). For 9 coils (3-phase, 3 coils/phase): multiples of 3 × something.

Specific stated values:
  6 coils: 8 magnets per flywheel (or 16 = 2×8)
  9 coils: 12 or 24 magnets per flywheel (24 = 2×12)

The underlying requirement: the number of magnets must produce alternating N-S pole faces that, when rotating, present a pole-face spatial frequency matching the spatial harmonic of the coil ring. For a 6-coil ring with 3-phase excitation, the fundamental spatial harmonic is the 3rd (3 N poles and 3 S poles alternating). 8 magnets produce 4 N-S pairs (4th harmonic), which does not exactly match the 3rd harmonic — this would produce sub-harmonic beating. Drew may be working with a configuration that is not at the spatial-harmonic resonance condition, which would explain why efficiency is low (6-10%).

====

## 3I/ATLAS Jet Power Conservation

From tweet note_tweet 2005590873623416947:
  "The total power of two jet-exhausts emerging from 3I/ATLAS remains conserved."
  "When the anti-tail jet (left) is weak, the other jet (right) is strong. When the anti-tail jet (left) is strong, the other jet (right) is weak."

Mathematical statement:
  P_jet1(t) + P_jet2(t) = P_total = constant

where P_jet1, P_jet2 are the powers of the two opposed jets. This anticorrelation (when one goes up, the other goes down, sum constant) is a strict conservation law behavior. For a natural sublimating comet, one expects only anti-solar activity P_jet1(t) ∝ illumination(t), with P_jet2 ≈ 0 at all times.

The observed anticorrelation would imply an active mechanism distributing a fixed internal power budget between two opposed jets — consistent with a propulsion/braking system as Drew claims, not consistent with solar-driven cometary outgassing.

Momentum delivered to object by jets over time dt:
  dp/dt = P_jet1/v_exhaust × n̂_1 + P_jet2/v_exhaust × n̂_2

where n̂_1 and n̂_2 are the unit vectors of the two jets (opposed: n̂_2 = -n̂_1). If P_jet1 ≠ P_jet2:
  dp/dt = (P_jet1 - P_jet2) / v_exhaust × n̂_1 ≠ 0

The object accelerates when P_jet1 ≠ P_jet2, and coasts at constant velocity when P_jet1 = P_jet2. This is the "accelerator and brake" analogy stated in the tweet.

## Note on Mathematical Content in Source Material

The source tweets and video transcriptions are from a public science communicator / experimental physicist (Dr. Horace Drew, aka RedCollie1). The mathematical content is primarily stated in qualitative physics terms rather than explicit equation form. The equations below are derived from the physical descriptions provided, using standard electromagnetic and mechanical physics consistent with what the source is describing. All equations are clearly labeled as to whether they are explicit in the source or implicit/derived from the physical description.

## 1. Magnetic Dipole Field Equations

Source: 3_1915353757367623681.txt (image description of dipole field diagram)

IMPLICIT (standard dipole physics described):

The magnetic field of a magnetic dipole with moment m located at origin:

B(r) = (mu_0 / 4*pi) * [ 3*(m · r_hat)*r_hat - m ] / r^3  (SI units, in free space)

Components in spherical coordinates (m = m_0 * z_hat):
B_r     = (mu_0 / 4*pi) * (2 * m_0 * cos(theta)) / r^3
B_theta = (mu_0 / 4*pi) * (m_0 * sin(theta)) / r^3
B_phi   = 0

The zero-field nodal plane (equator, theta = pi/2): B_r = 0, B_theta ≠ 0
The poles (theta = 0, pi): B_r maximum, B_theta = 0

The two-lobe iron-filing pattern traces the B_r component:
* Dense fillings near theta ≈ 0 and theta ≈ pi (near the poles, large B_r)
* Sparse fillings near theta ≈ pi/2 (equatorial plane)

The crop circle two-lobe structure is claimed to topologically reproduce this angular distribution.

---

## 2. 3-Phase Rotating Magnetic Field

Source: 1970471190230937728.yaml (note_tweet), 1945272410573541660.yaml, 2039176288649592984.yaml
IMPLICIT from physical description:

Three-coil symmetric 3-phase field at a point in space:
B_1(t) = B_0 * cos(omega*t) * x_hat                        (Phase U)
B_2(t) = B_0 * cos(omega*t - 2*pi/3) * x_hat              (Phase V, shifted 120 degrees in time)
B_3(t) = B_0 * cos(omega*t - 4*pi/3) * x_hat              (Phase W, shifted 240 degrees in time)

But arranged spatially at 120-degree angles:
B_1(t) = B_0 * cos(omega*t) * e_hat_1
B_2(t) = B_0 * cos(omega*t - 2*pi/3) * e_hat_2
B_3(t) = B_0 * cos(omega*t - 4*pi/3) * e_hat_3

where e_hat_1, e_hat_2, e_hat_3 are unit vectors at 0°, 120°, 240° in the XY-plane.

Total field:
B_total(t) = B_0 * [cos(omega*t) * e_hat_1 + cos(omega*t - 2*pi/3) * e_hat_2 + cos(omega*t - 4*pi/3) * e_hat_3]

For a balanced, symmetric 3-phase system:
B_total(t) = (3*B_0/2) * [cos(omega*t) * x_hat + sin(omega*t) * y_hat]

This is a vector of constant magnitude (3*B_0/2) rotating in the XY-plane at angular frequency omega.

For 9-coil configuration (U-V-W-U-V-W-U-V-W, equally spaced at 40-degree intervals):
The field has 3-fold spatial symmetry; to avoid parasitic torques, flywheel magnet count must be:
N_magnets = 2p, where p is pole count compatible with 9 stator slots.
Standard winding theory: for 9 slots, 3-phase: N = 6, 12, or 24 poles
Source specifies: 12 or 24 magnets per flywheel
